rcv.notes: Alaska elects U.S. senators by ranked-choice voting (instant runoff) in the general election, after a nonpartisan top-four primary (Ballot Measure 2, approved 2020; first used in 2022). Voters may rank up to five choices (four candidates plus a write-in). If no candidate has a majority of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated each round and those ballots move to their next choice; Alaska law continues tabulation until two candidates remain unless someone wins a first-round majority. Write-ins are tabulated individually only if all write-ins combined lead or are within 0.5% of the leader in round one (6 AAC 25.071). Ballot Measure No. 2 (24ESEG) on this Nov. 3 ballot would repeal the open primary and ranked-choice general elections and restore party primaries; the Nov. 3, 2026 Senate race itself is conducted under ranked-choice voting.
rcv.primary: Nonpartisan top-four primary held Aug. 18, 2026; top four advanced regardless of party. Fourth-place David Leslie withdrew by the Aug. 31 withdrawal deadline and fifth-place Gerald Heikes took his place.
rcv.tabulation: Election-night reports show first-choice (round 1) results only. Ranked-choice tabulation rounds begin after the last count of ballots on the 15th day after election day, i.e. Wed. Nov. 18, 2026, at the Director's Office in Juneau. Domestic mail ballots must arrive by Nov. 13 and overseas mail ballots by Nov. 18 (postmarked by Nov. 3). Target certification date: Nov. 25, 2026.

poll_close.notes: Polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Alaska Time zone (AKST, UTC-9; most of the state): 8 p.m. AKST = 05:00 UTC = 12:00 midnight ET (Nov. 4). Hawaii-Aleutian zone (HAST, UTC-10; Aleutian Islands west of Umnak Island): 8 p.m. HAST = 06:00 UTC = 1:00 a.m. ET (Nov. 4). Some media guides list 7 p.m. HAST for the western Aleutians; the Division's calendar gives only 7 a.m.-8 p.m. The Division says results are posted on the web after 9 p.m. (Alaska time, = 1 a.m. ET).

results_reporting.notes: Official results are published by state house district (HD01-HD40), with precincts inside each district; the Division posts a statewide summary (first choices only) and a Statement of Votes Cast per house district. In its district reports, absentee, early voting and questioned ballots appear as separate per-district rows ('District N - Absentee', 'District N - Early Voting', 'District N - Question'; format checked on the 2024 primary HD1 report). Absentee and questioned ballots keep being counted until Nov. 18. The Division also publishes the cast vote record (JSON). There are no counties; Alaska's boroughs are not reporting units.

rcv.notes: Kansas does not use ranked-choice voting. Under K.S.A. 25-702 the candidate with the highest number of votes is elected (plurality); there is no general-election runoff. A 2025 bill (SB 6) proposed an explicit ban on ranked-choice voting; its final status was not verified and it does not change the plurality rule.

poll_close.notes: Polls close at 7 p.m. local time. Most of Kansas (101 counties, Central time) closes at 7 p.m. CST = 8 p.m. ET. Four western counties on Mountain time (Greeley 20071, Hamilton 20075, Sherman 20181, Wallace 20199) close at 7 p.m. MST = 9 p.m. ET. By statute (K.S.A. 25-106) Central-time counties default to 7 a.m.-7 p.m. and may set other hours ending no later than 8 p.m. CST; Mountain-time counties default to 6 a.m.-6 p.m. MST and may run to 7 p.m. MST. Any voter in line at closing may vote. Note: Hamilton County shares its name with candidate Adam Hamilton; use the FIPS id, not the name, for county focus.

results_reporting.notes: Counties tabulate and report; the Secretary of State publishes statewide unofficial results on its election-night page (linked from votekansas.gov / sos.ks.gov elections page: https://ent.sos.ks.gov/kssos_ent.html). In 2024 the page went live at 5 p.m. CT and first results (mostly advance votes) appeared after polls closed; AP's first 2024 update came at 8:10 p.m. ET, the halfway point at 9:48 p.m. ET and the last election-night update at 3:45 a.m. ET (about 97% counted). Provisional ballots are counted at the county canvass after Election Day; official results follow certification by the State Board of Canvassers. Change from 2024: the Legislature did not authorize a mail-ballot grace period for 2026 (per the Secretary of State, June 29, 2026), so mail ballots arriving after polls close are not counted. More than 1 million votes were cast in the 2022 Senate race. Whether the election-night page reports precincts counted is unverified (the page returned a JavaScript challenge to our fetcher); precincts may be null.

ME.card_inclusion_note: Cards: Susan Collins (Republican nominee, incumbent) and Troy Jackson (Democratic nominee), the only two names printed on the ballot. Six declared write-in candidates are listed in declared_write_ins. Inclusion criteria and evidence: research/election/candidates.md.

rcv.notes: Maine uses ranked-choice voting in general elections only for federal offices (U.S. Senate, U.S. House, President) and in state primaries; not for governor or the legislature in general elections. The Senate ballot prints Collins and Jackson and has one write-in line; voters may rank the two printed candidates and one write-in. Only the six declared write-in candidates can receive counted write-in votes; a write-in for anyone else (including Graham Platner) is treated as a blank ranking, and the voter's next ranking can still count. Outright-win rule (21-A MRSA sec. 723-A(2), as amended by PL 2025 c. 363): a candidate wins without an RCV count if ranked first on more than 50% of ALL ballots cast for the office, including ballots whose first ranking is blank, overvoted or for an excluded candidate. Otherwise the count proceeds in rounds: each continuing ballot counts for its highest-ranked continuing candidate; when two or fewer continuing candidates remain, the candidate with the most votes wins; otherwise the last-place candidate is eliminated and a new round begins. Because blanks and declared write-ins count in the first-round denominator, an RCV tabulation can be triggered even though only two names are printed (as happened in the 2024 2nd Congressional District race with one declared write-in). Election-night numbers are first-choice counts only.
rcv.tabulation: If no candidate clears the outright-win threshold, the Secretary of State conducts a central RCV tabulation: ballots and tabulator memory devices from each municipality are securely transported to a central tabulation site in Augusta, processed and verified, and the RCV rounds are then run (the computation itself takes minutes). In the 2024 2nd District race the RCV tally was run 10 days after the election; the June 2026 primary RCV counts took more than a week. The Secretary of State must tabulate returns and submit a certified tabulation to the Governor within 20 days of the election (21-A MRSA sec. 722); the complete cast vote record is posted when certified results are reported (sec. 723-A(5-C)). Write-in candidates with under 5% are reported as 'others' in the official tabulation (sec. 722(1-A)).

poll_close.notes: All of Maine is in the Eastern time zone. Polls must close at 8 p.m. statewide (21-A MRSA sec. 626(2)); voters present at closing time may vote. Opening times vary by municipality (between 6 and 8 a.m.; municipalities under 500 population may open as late as 10 a.m.). Municipalities with population under 100 may close the polls once all registered voters have voted, so a few tiny towns may report before 8 p.m.

results_reporting.notes: Results are counted and reported by municipality (cities, towns, plantations), not by county; the stream aggregates municipal returns to Maine's 16 counties. On election night, municipal clerks report first-choice results after polls close at 8 p.m. (the Bangor Daily News compiles them from clerks and calls races with Decision Desk HQ); election officials post a paper copy of first-choice results at each voting place (21-A MRSA sec. 700). The Secretary of State's official tabulation is due within 20 days (sec. 722). The exact number of reporting municipalities/units for 2026 was not verified (null).

rcv.notes: Plurality winner; no ranked-choice voting and no general-election runoff. Ohio law (Ohio Rev. Code 3505.011, enacted 2026 per NCSL) prohibits ranked-choice voting except where home-rule provisions may allow it.

poll_close.notes: Polls open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. statewide; all of Ohio is in the Eastern time zone. Voters in line at 7:30 p.m. may still vote (R.C. 3501.32). Under a recent law change, absentee ballots must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day to be counted (Franklin County BOE notice); outstanding UOCAVA (military/overseas) and provisional ballots are handled in the official canvass.

results_reporting.notes: The Ohio Secretary of State publishes unofficial election-night results at 'Ohio Decides' (liveresults.ohiosos.gov), with county-level results and an Election Results XML feed in NIST SP 1500-100 format that updates every three minutes on election night; the page also lists outstanding UOCAVA absentee and provisional ballot counts by county ('Ballots Cast' tab). Precincts-reporting figures have been shown on the SOS site in past elections (cited in 2024 primary coverage) but were not confirmed on the 2026 page; check the XML feed. Results are unofficial until the official canvass about three weeks after the election. County boards of elections also post their own results.

rcv.notes: Michigan elects U.S. senators by plurality in a single general election; there is no runoff and no ranked-choice voting. State law currently prevents ranked-choice voting (several cities passed RCV ordinances that cannot be implemented). No RCV proposal is on the 2026-11-03 statewide ballot (Wikipedia lists only Proposal 1, constitutional convention, and Proposal 2, utility political contributions; not cross-checked with the Secretary of State).

poll_close.notes: Polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Most of Michigan is in the Eastern time zone (close 20:00 ET = 01:00 UTC Nov 4). Four Upper Peninsula counties on Central time - Dickinson, Gogebic, Iron and Menominee - close at 8 p.m. CT = 21:00 ET (02:00 UTC Nov 4). Voters in line at closing may still vote.

results_reporting.notes: About 1,600 city and township clerks count ballots and report to their county clerk; county clerk websites post unofficial results through the night (some show precinct-level progress). The Secretary of State's statewide page receives a county's results only after all of that county's precincts are fully reported, so it lags the county sites. In the 2026-08-04 primary the Secretary of State said unofficial results were expected to be fully reported about 24 hours after polls closed; statewide unofficial results are linked from mi.gov/vote. A statewide precincts-reporting count is not consistently published, so precincts may need to be null at the state level.

declared_write_ins.note: No declared write-in candidates for U.S. Senate listed (write-in filing deadline 2026-10-23).
